statement.p: For each given graph of y = f(x), sketch an approximate graph of its derivative function, y = f'(x), on the axes immediately below. The scale of the grid for the graph of f is 1 \times 1; assume the horizontal scale of the grid for the graph of f' is identical to that for f. If necessary, adjust and label the vertical scale on the axes for f'.

When you are finished with all 8 graphs, write several sentences that describe your overall process for sketching the graph of the derivative function, given the graph the original function. What are the values of the derivative function that you tend to identify first? What do you do thereafter? How do key traits of the graph of the derivative function exemplify properties of the graph of the original function?

description.p: This image consists of 4 sets of axes arranged in two rows and two columns. There is no scale on any of the axes. In the top left, there is a cubic function f that crosses the x-axis three times. In the top right, there is a decreasing exponential function g that is always positive and that approaches the x-axis as x increases without bound. Beneath each of these two figures there are similar-sized blank coordinate axes for plotting f' and g'.

This image consists of 4 sets of axes arranged in two rows and two columns. There is no scale on any of the axes. In the top left, there is a function p that looks like \sin(x) that crosses the x-axis three times to the left of the origin, at the origin, and three times to the right of the origin. In the top right, there is a function q that has a horizontal asymptote of y = 0 in both directions, is always negative for x \lt 0 and always positive for x \gt 0 and that passes through the origin. Beneath each of these two figures there are similar-sized blank coordinate axes for plotting p' and q'.

This image consists of 4 sets of axes arranged in two rows and two columns. There is no scale on any of the axes. In the top left, there is a function r that is always increasing but occasionally levels off to have a horizontal tangent line, once to the left of x=0, and once to the right of x=0. In the top right, there is a function s that looks like the absolute value function, but shifted slightly down; in other words, the graph of s is a V with the point of the V located at (0,-3). Beneath each of these two figures there are similar-sized blank coordinate axes for plotting r' and s'.

This image consists of 4 sets of axes arranged in two rows and two columns. There is no scale on any of the axes. In the top left, there is a function w that looks like the absolute value of the sine function: the graph is a sequence of adjacenthumps. In the top right, there is a function z that looks like the rational function y = \frac{1}{x}. Beneath each of these two figures there are similar-sized blank coordinate axes for plotting w' and z'.

hint.p: Points where the slope of the tangent line is equal to zero are particularly important. Try finding these points first in your effort to plot y = f'(x) and plotting those zero values on the axes where you'll graph y = f'(x).

description.p: This image consists of 4 sets of axes arranged in two rows and two columns. There is no scale on any of the axes. In the top left, there is a cubic function f that crosses the x-axis three times. In the top right, there is a decreasing exponential function g that is always positive and that approaches the x-axis as x increases without bound.

Beneath each of these two figures the graphs of f' and g' are shown. On the bottom left, the graph of f' is an upward-opening parabola that crosses the x-axis at the locations where f has horizontal tangent lines. On the bottom right, the graph of g' is an exponential function that is always negative, always increasing, and that approaches the x-axis as the value of x increases.

This image consists of 4 sets of axes arranged in two rows and two columns. There is no scale on any of the axes. In the top left, there is a function p that looks like \sin(x) that crosses the x-axis three times to the left of the origin, at the origin, and three times to the right of the origin. In the top right, there is a function q that has a horizontal asymptote of y = 0 in both directions, is always negative for x \lt 0 and always positive for x \gt 0 and that passes through the origin.

Beneath each of these two figures there are respective plots of p' and q'. The graph of p' looks similar to the cosine function, and crosses the x-axis everywhere the graph of p has a horizontal tangent line. The graph of q' is positive on the approximate interval -1.5 \lt x \lt 1.5 and with its largest value at x = 0. At approximately x = 1.5, q'(x) = 0, and then moving right, q'(x) becomes more negative for a little ways, and then the derivative function starts to get less negative and approach the horizontal axis. To the left of x = -1.5, the graph of q' behaves similarly. Overall, the graph of q' is symmetric about the y-axis.

This image consists of 4 sets of axes arranged in two rows and two columns. There is no scale on any of the axes. In the top left, there is a function r that is always increasing but occasionally levels off to have a horizontal tangent line, once to the left of x=0, and once to the right of x=0. In the top right, there is a function s that looks like the absolute value function, but shifted slightly down; in other words, the graph of s is a V with the point of the V located at (0,-3).

Beneath each of these two figures are respective plots of r' and s'. On the left, the graph of r' looks similar to the function y = \cos(x) + 1: a sinusoidal function that is always nonnegative; note that r'(x) = 0 wherever r(x) has horizontal tangent lines. On the right, the graph of s'(x) is the piecewise function that satisfies s'(x) = -1 for x \lt 0 and s'(x) = +1 for x \gt 0, with s'(0) being undefined due to the sharp corner in the graph of s at x = 0.

This image consists of 4 sets of axes arranged in two rows and two columns. There is no scale on any of the axes. In the top left, there is a function w that looks like the absolute value of the sine function: the graph is a sequence of adjacenthumps. In the top right, there is a function z that looks like the rational function y = \frac{1}{x}.

Beneath each of these two figures are respective plots of w' and z'. On the left, note that w'(x) is undefined at each of the sharp corners on w, and since the graph of w is periodic, so is the graph of w'. Each piece of w' falls from a high point corresponding to the lefthand start of the corresponding hump on w, crosses the x-axis at a location aligned with the top of the corresponding hump on w, and falls to its lowest value at a location corresponding to the righthand end of the corresponding hump on w. On the right, the graph of z' is that of a rational function that is always negative with a horizontal asymptote of y = 0 and a vertical asymptote of x = 0.
